summary: A periodic list prepared by the RFC Editor showing the state of Internet protocol standards at the time of publication, as described in the standards process of RFC 2026. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 2700.

eli5.summary: It is a report card for Internet rules, listing which ones were officially approved at that moment. Newer report cards replaced it.

subtitle: A snapshot of which Internet protocols had official status as of March 2000.

tldr.problem: The Internet Engineering Task Force needed a way to publish which protocols had been officially standardized and at what level, so implementers knew which to build into products.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2600 lists every Internet protocol in sections organized by status (Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Historic), with its number, the RFC(s) defining it, and its STD number.
tldr.outcome: This was a point-in-time report published periodically to reflect the state of standardization. It was marked Historic and replaced by RFC 2700.

facts.label: Highest STD number in this edition

today: RFC 2600 is marked Historic and has been replaced by RFC 2700 and subsequent updates. The Internet Standards process continues to update this list as new protocols reach standard status, old ones are retired, and new editions are published periodically.

sections.title: What This Document Is
sections.content:
RFC 2600, the Internet Official Protocol Standards, is a snapshot of the standardization state of protocols used in the Internet as of March 2000. It is published by the RFC Editor in accordance with the Internet Standards Process defined in RFC 2026, which lays out how protocols move through different maturity levels.

This is a meta-document: it does not define a new protocol but rather documents the status of all known protocols. It lists contacts for the IETF, IANA, and the RFC Editor, and provides a table of every protocol with its RFC numbers, STD number (if assigned), and current status.
sections.eli5: This is a report about all the rules for the Internet. It says which rules are official, which are being tested, and which are retired.

sections.title: Levels of Standardization
sections.content:
Protocols in RFC 2600 are organized into five status categories. Internet Standard protocols (marked STD followed by a number) are fully approved and recommended for use. Examples include TCP (STD 7), UDP (STD 6), DNS (STD 13), and SNMP (STD 15). These have gone through the entire approval process and are considered stable.

Draft Standard protocols are those that have been approved but are undergoing final testing and refinement before moving to full Standard status. Proposed Standard protocols are newer and not yet recommended for widespread use, though they are available for implementers to try. Experimental protocols are those where the IETF wanted to document an idea or technique but had not fully committed to standardization.

Historic protocols are those that were once used or proposed but are now obsolete. RFC 2600 itself falls into this category after being replaced by later updates. Some Historic protocols were replaced by newer versions (like older RIP versions), while others simply fell out of use.
sections.eli5: Protocols have different levels: official rules that everyone should use, rules being tested, experimental ideas, and old retired rules nobody uses anymore.

sections.title: Common Protocols Listed
sections.content:
RFC 2600 lists the core Internet infrastructure protocols. The fundamentals include IP (STD 5, RFC 791), ICMP for error messages, and IGMP for multicast group management. For transport, TCP and UDP are listed as Standards. For applications, TELNET, FTP, SMTP, and DNS are all Standards, along with administrative tools like NTP (network time synchronization).

The document also includes less visible but critical protocols like ARP (address resolution), which maps IP addresses to physical network addresses, and RARP (reverse ARP), which was used by diskless machines to learn their own IP address. Network management protocols like SNMP are included, along with various transmission standards for moving IP datagrams over Ethernet, PPP, FDDI, and other physical media.

The complete table in RFC 2600 spans dozens of protocols, organized both by their STD assignment number and by their RFC number for easy lookup.
sections.eli5: It lists famous rules like TCP and IP, plus less famous but important ones like DNS, SMTP for email, and SNMP for managing routers.

sections.title: How Protocols Get Standardized
sections.content:
RFC 2600 reflects the Internet Standards Process outlined in RFC 2026. A protocol starts as a Proposed Standard when the IETF working group has reviewed it and the IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) has approved it. At this stage there is no commitment to long-term support.

A Proposed Standard can advance to Draft Standard if it has been in use for at least four months, has been reviewed by at least two independent implementations, and has resolved known issues. It stays in Draft Standard for at least four months. Finally, the IESG can advance a protocol to Internet Standard (full standard) only after it has existed as a Draft Standard for at least four months and the IESG and IAB agree it is ready.

The STD (Internet Standard) number is assigned to a protocol when it reaches Internet Standard status. If a protocol is updated or refined in a new RFC, it keeps the same STD number but the obsoletes and updates relationships are tracked to show the history.
sections.eli5: New rules start as experiments, then are tested for four months. If they work, they get tested again. Finally, if everyone agrees, they become official rules.
